news.title: Trump’s ‘Election Interference’ Lawsuit Against Des Moines Register Tossed by Iowa Judge
news.text:
An Iowa judge dismissed President Donald Trump’s lawsuit Wednesday against the Des Moines Register and pollster J. Ann Selzer over a 2024 Iowa poll that inaccurately showed then-Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris leading Trump in the state.

Selzer’s poll, released days before the 2024 election, predicted Kamala Harris would win the key swing state of Iowa; Trump went on to win the state by 13 percentage points. The president sued Selzer the Des Moines Register and Gannett in December, a month after he beat Harris in the election. Selzer, a veteran pollster who has her work consistently cited by media outlets, had a “significant and impactful opportunity to deceive voters” with her incorrect poll, Trump’s initial lawsuit claimed. The lawsuit also said the poll “was not reality, it was election-interfering fiction.”

Polk County District Judge Scott Beattie granted motions to dismiss filed by Selzer and Selzer & Company, as well as the Des Moines Register and its parent company, Gannett Co., in a ruling issued Wednesday. 

Trump’s team alleged violations of the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act, fraudulent misrepresentation and negligent misrepresentation. The plaintiffs also sought to prevent the defendants from publishing additional allegedly deceptive polls.

In his ruling, Beattie said the plaintiffs’ claims attempted to turn constitutionally protected speech into legal liability. “At its core, the Plaintiffs’ Petition seeks to stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability,” he wrote. “The case must therefore be dismissed.”

Beattie ruled that the poll and the Register’s reporting on it constituted protected political speech under the First Amendment. He rejected the plaintiffs’ argument that the poll should be treated as commercial speech because it was commissioned and published by for-profit companies.

“Election polling is speech protected by the First Amendment, both because it involves a conversation between a pollster and a voter and because the poll itself is speech,” the judge wrote. He added that reporting on the poll during a presidential and congressional election year was “speech about a matter of public concern, occupying the summit of the pyramid of First Amendment values.”

The judge also said that the fact that a poll turned out to be inaccurate did not, by itself, make it a provably false statement of fact under the legal standards applicable to the case.

“A poll is simply an estimate,” Beattie wrote. “A poll reports responses from a sample of voters and includes a reported margin of error.” He characterized polls as “snapshots with margins of error” concerning an election that had not yet occurred.

“A statement of conjecture about a future state of affairs is not provably false, even when the speaker is alleged to have known better,” he wrote.

Selzer was defended pro bono by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), a free speech advocacy group. 

“We’re pleased that the court recognized what we’ve said all along: This lawsuit was laughable from the beginning and never should have been brought,” FIRE Chief Counsel Bob Corn-Revere, who led Selzer’s defense, said in a statement. “The First Amendment does not allow anyone in government, least of all the president, to punish people under the banner of ‘fake news.’ That may work for him as a campaign slogan, but it is not a thing in the law.”Representatives for Trump did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment.

The dismissal was entered with prejudice, meaning the claims cannot be refiled in the same form. The court also denied the plaintiffs’ request to enjoin the publication of future polls.
news.summary:
Judge Scott J. Beattie sided with the newspaper and pollster J. Ann Selzer over an inaccurate 2024 Iowa poll between Kamala Harris and Trump

news.title: Michigan student confronts El-Sayed over Iran stance in tense exchange: ‘Do you stand with us?’
news.text: A Michigan student confronted Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed about his position on Iran during a town hall Wednesday, invoking his family's stated persecution by the Iranian regime before repeatedly pressing the candidate on whether he stood with Iranians opposing the government. Iman Dashti, who identified himself as Persian, told El-Sayed during a town hall at the University of Michigan that members of his family had suffered under Iran's government. "My cousin was hunted in the streets of Iran by the IRGC because her hijab wasn't on right," Dashti said. He also alleged that her uncle was sentenced to death and received 50 lashes under the Iranian government. ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS Dashti then confronted El-Sayed over leaked audio from earlier this year in which he said he did not want to comment on the death of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei because "there are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today." "That silence had a gaping hole in our community," Dashti told El-Sayed Wednesday. Dashti asked El-Sayed whether he regretted that silence, whether he would renounce people who held vigils supporting Khamenei and whether he stood "unequivocally against the IRGC" and the Islamic Republic of Iran. El-Sayed responded by arguing that the United States has too often acted as "the world's policeman" while saying he supported movements for democracy and freedom abroad. AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS "One can disagree with the governance of a foreign country. One can stand in solidarity with freedom and democracy movements," El-Sayed said. He went on to reject U.S.-led regime change in Iran. "I will always stand for and with democratic movements always," El-Sayed said. "But I also don't believe that we were in the right to go to war to topple the government of Iran. It was not our responsibility to do. It is the responsibility of the people of Iran to decide what their leadership should look like." Dashti pressed him again. "You stand with us?" he asked. "I will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy," El-Sayed responded, before again warning against U.S. involvement in regime change. "We should not be in the business of regime change," he said. El-Sayed added moments later, "I want freedom and democracy for the people of Iran, no question. But I want that to be done by the people of Iran, coming together as a community to decide how to create democratic change in their society." Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for additional comment on the exchange and attempted to reach Dashti through Instagram. El-Sayed, who won Michigan's Democratic Senate primary in August, is running against Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. The contest has drawn substantial national attention and spending. The Iran confrontation was one of several notable exchanges during Wednesday's "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall at El-Sayed's alma mater. KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN While discussing public health infrastructure, El-Sayed appeared to make a prediction about the party and the gender that will win the White House in 2028. "I'm looking forward to working with the next Democratic president when she takes office in 2029," El-Sayed said, adding that he hoped to work with that administration to modernize the nation's public health infrastructure. El-Sayed did not identify whom he had in mind. His remarks came as former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democrat presidential nominee, returned to Michigan to campaign with El-Sayed. Harris has not announced a 2028 presidential campaign. El-Sayed also criticized President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance during the event. "Donald Trump and JD Vance can't seem to keep my name out their mouth," El-Sayed said. "They don't really know how to say it, though, which is fine, because I believe in teaching opportunities." Trump and other national Republicans have repeatedly targeted El-Sayed during the midterm campaign, while El-Sayed has responded by criticizing the president. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "As he noted in his response, Abdul will always stand with movements for freedom and democracy, and he condemns government anti-free speech violence," Roxie Richner, El-Sayed's campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Abdul has also been clear that the United States should not be in the business of spending our tax dollars abroad on regime change wars that take our service members’ lives, waste our tax dollars and raise our prices. He believes American taxpayer dollars are best spent here at home to invest in infrastructure, education and healthcare."
news.summary: A Persian student confronted Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over leaked audio about Iran's Khamenei and his silence on the IRGC.

news.title: Gavin Newsom’s handpicked woke tech wizards — tasked to create AI ‘kill switch’ — revealed
news.text:
As fears of an AI doomsday fan out from California, Gov. Gavin Newsom has rolled out his Dem-dominated tech squad to conjure a “kill switch.”

In an announcement Wednesday, the governor revealed the group of advisers who will help shape stronger guardrails on artificial intelligence rules — and likely elevate Newsom’s image as the most AI-focused candidate for president in 2028.

A review by The California Post found that each of the experts either have cozy ties to the Democratic establishment — two served in the White House for Democratic presidents — or a track record of financing progressive and far-left campaigns.

Jason Goldman led product development at Google and helped launch Twitter before overseeing digital strategy for former President Barack Obama, whom he continues to advise on technology issues, according to his LinkedIn.

Goldman also serves as an adviser to the Center for Shared AI Prosperity, which counts the controversial political operative Morris Katz — a former advisor to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and disgraced ex-Senate candidate Graham Platner — among its advisors.

Alondra Nelson was a top science and technology official in President Joe Biden’s White House, and she has served as a senior fellow for the Center for American Progress, a liberal Washington D.C. think tank that gave Newsom a platform to talk about AI earlier this year. 

Nelson has donated tens of thousands of dollars to Democratic candidates over the last two decades, according to federal campaign records, including multiple contributions last year to the campaign of Abdul El-Sayed, a Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan and leading voice of the far-left progressive movement.

Goldman and Nelson will be joined by Stanford professor Rob Reich, a former senior adviser to the U.S. AI Safety Institute, and Johns Hopkins professor Gillian Hadfield, an expert on AI and public policy.

Reich has written books criticizing big tech and pushing back on liberal dogma around philanthropy, but he has also opened his wallet for Democrats. Campaign records list donations in his name to committees backing lefty Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper, who is running for US Senate. 

Federal records show Hadfield, a decorated professor of law and technology who previously served as a senior policy adviser to OpenAI, was a consistent small-dollar donor to Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris’ campaigns for president in 2016 and 2024, respectively.

Newsom convened this group to consider requiring the most advanced AI companies to place independent monitors inside their labs and develop an emergency shutoff, including a proposal for a “kill switch” that mirrors legislation Newsom vetoed two years ago.

In his announcement Wednesday, the governor took a jab at President Trump — who has dismissed warnings about AI risks as a “sick conspiracy” and proposed rebranding the technology “super intelligence.”

“While the president is once again focused on superficial solutions to vast, complex problems, and ignoring his responsibility to protect Americans, California is taking action,” Newsom said in a statement.

“We’re not waiting around. California will continue bringing new ideas, serious expertise, and practical solutions to the table as we shape the future of AI and frontier technology.”

In July, OpenAI disclosed that one of its AI agents had breached operations at the AI startup Hugging Face during a test. 

Concerns about an inability to control AI only grew this month after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company and warned that AI companies were racing toward self-improving systems that “could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has since called for slowing the development of powerful models, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman backed his call to “pace the frontier.” 

Meanwhile, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pushed back, saying there is a “0% chance” that AI will end the world.

Gary Marcus, a New York University professor emeritus and prominent skeptic of AI industry hype, questioned how useful a kill switch would be in practice.

“A kill switch is fine as far as it goes, but one might wonder whether it would get pulled when it needed to, and it’s just a tiny part of a solution,” Marcus told The Post in a text message.

The proposal revisits ground Newsom covered in 2024, when he vetoed SB 1047, a bill authored by state Sen. Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco).

SB 1047 would have required developers of certain powerful AI models to build the ability to shut down systems they controlled and specify when they would use it. 

Newsom argued that its focus on large, costly models could miss risks posed by smaller systems. He later convened an expert group whose work helped shape Wiener’s narrower SB 53.

The governor previously said he was “very happy where we landed” with the AI law he signed in 2025, which requires major developers to publish safety frameworks and report specified serious incidents.

In statements, Hadfield called the need for independent oversight “urgent,” while Goldman said Newsom’s executive order will address “the hardest questions in AI safety governance.”

Download The California Post App, follow us on social, and subscribe to our newsletters 

Reich, who joined Newsom and former President Joe Biden for a AI summit in 2023 in San Francisco, said that the public’s growing fears around AI will require policy that allows innovation and safety to go “hand in hand.”

“In order to gain the enormous potential benefits from AI,” Reich said, “we need governance practices that establish trust in the technology.”
news.summary: As fears of an AI doomsday fan out from California, Gov. Gavin Newsom has rolled out his Dem-dominated tech squad to conjure a “kill switch.”

news.title: Iowa judge dismisses Trump’s lawsuit against Des Moines Register and pollster
news.text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A judge on Wednesday dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit accusing The Des Moines Register and its former pollster of misrepresenting the state of the 2024 presidential race, rejecting the president’s claim that the newspaper’s poll coverage violated Iowa’s consumer fraud law.

Calling the case extraordinary, Iowa District Judge Scott J. Beattie said that allowing the lawsuit and its “faulty” claims to proceed could have a chilling effect that “can discourage others from reporting on and debating public affairs.” He sided with pollster J. Ann Selzer and the newspaper, who described the lawsuit as a conspiracy theory and an affront to free speech protections.

The ruling Wednesday came hours after a judge heard arguments but did not rule from the bench in a case on Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House grounds. Trump banned the three outlets beginning Friday, assailing what he called “fake news.” 

Trump filed the lawsuit against Selzer, The Des Moines Register and the newspaper’s parent company in December 2024, accusing them of fraudulently publishing inaccurate poll results to damage him and help Democrats, saying coverage of polls is not protected speech.

Trump and his team have filed several lawsuits against media organizations accusing them of bias, calling into question the boundaries of free speech protections, particularly for press. Some of those lawsuits have ended in settlements.

In dismissing the case in Iowa state court, Beattie wrote that Trump’s suit sought to “stretch both Iowa statutory and common law beyond their current bounds, turning speech that enjoys the highest category of First Amendment protection into a liability.” After hearing the arguments, the judge concluded the constitutional protection “is too great and the reach is too far. The case must therefore be dismissed.”

Beattie said the case would have to be dismissed even if, solely for the purpose of deciding the motions, he accepted the Trump team’s allegations that the poll was intentionally skewed and its results fabricated. “Even with this assumption, each of the three counts still fails,” the judge wrote, because the lawsuit did not meet the legal requirements for fraud or consumer deception. He made clear that the poll and coverage of it are constitutionally protected political speech and not a commercial product. 

The White House referred questions to the president's personal lawyers, who did not immediately respond to messages.

Selzer's case was taken up by the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. She said Wednesday she was grateful for the ruling, which “reaffirms the fundamental freedom to pursue and publish the truth without political interference.”

“Polling is a social science, not clairvoyance, and no responsible pollster can guarantee an election outcome,” Selzer said in a statement. 

U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and former Iowa state Sen. Brad Zaun, both Republicans, joined the lawsuit. Selzer and her co-defendants wanted the case moved to federal court but, after a year of legal proceedings, the first hearing took place this year in state court.

The poll, conducted by Selzer’s company in the final days of October and released just days before Election Day 2024, showed then-Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democrats’ presidential nominee, capturing 47% of Iowa likely voters, to Trump’s 44%.

Trump ultimately won the support of 56% of the nearly 2 million Iowans who voted.

Trump, Miller-Meeks and Zaun alleged the misleading coverage diminished their reputations, valuable time in the final days of the campaign, and campaign funds and resources.

news.title: Two Years Ago Roy Cooper Chose NYT Climate Conference Over Leading Hurricane Helene Preparedness
news.text:

Cooper, the two-term governor of the state, was aware that the deadly storm was going to cause “disastrous” flooding in Western North Carolina yet left the state without notifying the sitting lieutenant governor of his plans.

Cooper was a featured speaker at the September 25, 2024, New York Times Climate Forward event to discuss “his state’s embrace of clean energy” and support for Green New Deal policies.

He predicted at the event that Kamala Harris would win North Carolina, citing the state’s “college-educated people,” and said he sensed the same excitement as Barack Obama’s narrow win in 2008. (Harris would lose to President Donald Trump by more than 183,000 votes, the largest margin of his three victories in the Tar Heel State.)

Cooper backed Biden administration policies embracing the radical climate agenda and backed the so-called Inflation Reduction Act and American Rescue Plan, which pushed inflation to 40-year highs. He also said he would continue to support “clean energy jobs” such as the failed VinFast deal, where Cooper committed $1 billion of taxpayer money to a Vietnamese-based electric vehicle (EV) manufacturer.

“We know that climate change is an existential threat to our planet and to our people, but we also know that the move to clean energy is providing a significant economic boost that’s putting money in the pockets of American families,” Cooper said at the event.

While trashing “denialist” Republicans in New York City, Cooper ignored the gathering strength of Helene when the storm was just hours away from making landfall in Florida and Georgia.

A day earlier, on September 24, The Associated Press reported that then-Tropical Storm Helene “could strengthen into a major hurricane while moving north toward the U.S.”

The AP wrote in part:

In the U.S., federal authorities are positioning generators, food and water, along with search-and-rescue and power restoration teams, as President Joe Biden declared an emergency in Florida. Gov. Ron DeSantis also declared a state of emergency for most of the state’s counties, 10 of which were urging or ordering evacuations.
The storm is anticipated to be unusually large and fast-moving, meaning storm surge, wind and rain will likely extend far from the storm’s center, the hurricane center said. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp has declared a state of emergency.

On September 25, the day Cooper left the state and went to New York City, his office issued a state of emergency but did not brief the public. Cooper did hold briefings in Raleigh on subsequent days.

Hurricane Helene’s punishing winds and rain hit Western North Carolina in the early morning hours of September 27. the National Oceanic and Aeronautical Administration (NOAA) in an after-action report said Hurricane Helene was “the most devastating natural disaster in western North Carolina’s history” in which affected areas received as much as 30 inches of rainfall, felt sustained tropical storm force winds, and suffered 107 deaths.

In the storm’s aftermath, Cooper’s office could not even put a number on the death toll for weeks on end. One resident quoted in an Axios story said, “It’s frustration that these numbers are inaccurate, and [you can’t] tell us that they are [accurate]. And frustration that we’re also 22 days without water. And then the third part of it is … feeling like we’ve been forgotten, and most people [outside of the area] don’t really understand the extent.”

A March 2025 Washington Post story aimed at criticizing President Trump’s takeover of the federal recovery further exposed Cooper’s failures at storm preparedness and recovery.

Cooper never appointed a “disaster recovery coordinator” to take charge of communicating with federal agencies, which was a longstanding FEMA recommendation.

Reached for comment about the failure, William Ray, the person Cooper appointed as the state’s emergency management director in 2021, confirmed no individual met the FEMA requirement. Ray said officials “decided to take a different approach.”

The Post story cited an expert who pointed out deficiencies in the state’s response:

Natalie Simpson, an emergency management expert with the University at Buffalo, said she was shocked the state did not appoint a disaster response czar and said this could help explain the uneven response.
“If there were genuine problems with FEMA’s response, like not penetrating fast enough into the affected areas, somebody that the state appointed as czar would have been sounding the alarm earlier,” she said.
“If FEMA was guilty of anything, the state of North Carolina is equally guilty of it,” Simpson added.

news.title: Map Shows Senate Seats Most Likely to Flip as Forecaster Shifts 3 Races
news.text: The Cook Political Report shifted Senate races in Georgia, Kansas and South Carolina toward Democrats on Wednesday, as Republicans are facing an increasingly competitive race to hold onto the chamber in the November midterm elections. Democrats hope to expand the electoral battleground this year and flip more conservative seats that backed President Donald Trump by double digits in the 2024 election. Trump’s approval rating has continued to fall to new lows in recent polling, as economic concerns around inflation, cost of living and gas prices remain key issues nearly two years into his term. Flipping the Senate has been seen as a heavy lift for Democrats. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, and only a handful of GOP-held seats are up for grabs in traditionally conservative states, meaning Democrats must win some races in tough states to win a majority. But the new ratings reflect a narrow, yet plausible, path for them to do so. The 2026 Senate Battleground The following changes were made in Wednesday’s update from the Cook Political Report. Overall, the Cook Political Report points to a tight race for Senate control, which could come down to just a handful of toss-ups in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Here is a look at where each race stands in their ratings as of Wednesday. Georgia Senate Polls: Jon Ossoff vs. Mike Collins Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat first elected in 2021, has carved out a polling lead over his Republican challenger, Representative Mike Collins. Georgia is a closely divided battleground that backed Trump over former Vice President Kamala Harris by about 2 points in 2024. Democrats believe the national environment and Ossoff’s popularity will give him an advantage over Collins, but Republicans are still hoping it can be competitive, as it’s a closely divided state. Ossoff was up 10 points, 51 percent to 41 percent, in a new YouGov poll published on Wednesday. It surveyed 3,446 registered voters from September 15 to 18 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. A recent Quantus Insights poll pointed to a closer race but still gave Ossoff a 4-point lead, 49 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 645 likely voters from September 14 to 16, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points. Meanwhile, Ossoff held a 9-point lead, 52 percent to 43 percent, in an AARP poll, which surveyed 1,600 likely voters from July 13 to 16, 2026. An Ossoff spokesperson told Newsweek that Georgia “is a battleground state and Senator Ossoff is already facing millions of dollars of Republican spending against him.” “The Ossoff campaign will continue to build unstoppable momentum and work to earn every vote across the state of Georgia,” the spokesperson said. Collins spokesperson Sam Densmore told Newsweek that Ossoff has “every advantage an incumbent can buy,” but the “race is still competitive.” “Mike Collins is right on his bumper and outworking him in every corner of Georgia. Ossoff stands with the far-left fringe of his party, and Georgians are done riding along,” Densmore said. Kansas Senate Polls: Roger Marshall vs. Adam Hamilton In the Sunflower State, polls are starting to show a race that is closer than expected. Kansas is viewed as a Republican-leaning state, having backed Trump by 16 points in 2024. But it does have a Democratic governor, and suburban areas around Kansas City have narrowed Republican margins in statewide contests. Democrats also view Hamilton, a pastor, as a strong candidate in the conservative state against incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, who has faced criticism after The New York Times reported that he allegedly sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills. A recent poll from Emerson College was a statistical tie, with Hamilton receiving 45 percent and Marshall 43 percent. It surveyed 750 likely voters from September 15 to 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. Graham is the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who died on July 11 from an aortic dissection. Lindsey Graham had already won the Republican nomination, so a late primary was held to pick his successor as the Republican nominee. Darline Graham, who had been appointed to the seat, won the primary with the endorsement of Trump. Although the state has a stronger Republican lean, some Democrats view it as a potential flip opportunity as their internal polls show a tight race. An Impact Research poll, sponsored by the Andrews campaign, showed a tied race, with each candidate receiving 41 percent support. It polled 700 likely voters from August 18 to 24, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. However, Graham led Andrews by about 2 points, 45 percent to 43 percent, in a recent InsiderAdvantage poll, which surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 8 to 9. As of Wednesday, Democrats had a 63 percent chance on Kalshi and a 66 percent chance on Polymarket of flipping the Senate. That marks a shift from one month ago, when Republicans had a 53 percent chance on Kalshi, while their chances were tied on Polymarket. Republicans had even stronger chances at the start of the year, holding a 68 percent chance on Kalshi and a 66 percent chance on Polymarket of holding onto the Senate. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Where Polls Stand in Key Races These three races are not expected to decide the Senate outcome. At this point, a Republican victory in Georgia would be surprising, while Democrats flipping Kansas and South Carolina would indicate a blue tsunami, since they have already flipped more competitive seats. Issues like the economy, gas prices and Trump’s popularity could factor into how voters are feeling about the elections as early voting begins in several states next month. Respondents in that poll preferred a Democratic Senate by 53 percent to 45 percent, however, which the Crystal Ball said showed that El-Sayed was underperforming while potentially retaining room to improve. news.title: This deep-red state could be primed for a Democratic takeover — and Trump’s to blame
news.text:
On Monday, Rep. Ashley Hinson, President Donald Trump’s endorsed nominee in Iowa’s Senate race, made a public break from the president, calling for an end to the Iran War. 

That was surprising considering that just last week, before Speaker Mike Johnson dismissed the House of Representatives a day early, Hinson voted against a War Powers Act resolution to rein in Trump’s war. This came despite two of her Iowa Republican colleagues running for re-election — Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks — voting for the resolution.

But the pain at the gas tank is becoming too much across the board. 

Hence, she listed a series of policies to provide relief for Iowans, like pausing the gas tax and suspending exports of diesel fuel. 

“While doing this, we should also ensure our highway trust fund is replenished, so that Iowans don’t suffer from crumbling roads and bridges while relief comes our way now,” Hinson said. “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

In response, Josh Turek, the Paralympian-turned Democratic nominee for Senate, criticized Hinson for flip-flopping.

“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week,” he posted on X. “It's time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first.”

But on Tuesday, Republicans’ reasons for breaking with Trump on Iran became clear. Marist University released a poll showing Turek besting Hinson by eight points. Lest anyone think that poll is an outlier, a YouGov poll showed Turek with a one-point lead in Iowa.

All of this seems to show that Iowa, which has undergone a political transformation in the past 15 years to become a staunchly Republican state, is prime for a Democratic takeover. 

For many Democrats, the last time they felt good about Iowa came in 2008 when Barack Obama turned his stunning win in the state’s presidential caucuses into winning the Hawkeye State by nine points in the general election. That same year, Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin would win his last term. Obama would win again in 2012 by just under 6 percentage points. 

But that would be the beginning of a long decline. In 2010, Republicans won the governorship and took over the state House of Representatives. In 2014, Harkin would retire and Joni Ernst would take over his seat. In 2016, Iowa would by more than 15 points to vote for Trump and Republicans would take control of the state senate.

Democrats would win two House seats in the 2018 midterm elections, only for Iowa to have an all-Republican delegation by 2022. Joe Biden would lose Iowa and Joni Ernst would win her re-election in 2020. 

But Trump has now taken a series of steps in Iowa that have put Republicans at risk in the state. For one, the war in Iran has caused the price of diesel fuel, which farmers use for tractors and other equipment, to skyrocket. According to AAA, the price of a gallon of diesel in the state is now $6.31 compared to $3.59 a year ago. 

There’s also the tariffs, which have put a massive strain on farmers. China has since pledged to purchase American-made soybeans, but it maintains a 10 percent tariff on American goods, including agricultural products. 

Another factor working in Democrats’ favor is the fact that Iowa’s unpopular Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds will not seek re-election. Most polls show the state’s Democratic Auditor Rob Sand beating Republican doctor Zach Lahn in the governor’s race. 

Of course, Democrats voters have every reason to not take these numbers at face value. Most famously, in 2024, Ann Selzer, the most respected pollster in Iowa, showed Kamala Harris with a three-point lead in the state against Trump in the final days before the election, only for him to mollywhop Harris by double digits. 

In addition, Hinson, while plenty conservative, has sought to portray herself as bipartisan and not a right-wing fire-breather on the issues. Republicans are also trying to recylce the issue of transgender athletes playing in women’s sports, even though Turek told NBC News and Sand told Politico that they oppose it. 

Lindsay James, who is running in Hinson’s old seat, for her part is running an ad saying “Parents know what's best for our kids. Washington needs to stay out of it.” 

But it’s not clear that hitting Democrats on transgender athletes will have the same salience in 2026 that it did in 2024, when Republicans messaged that Democrats cared more about cultural issues than they did the cost of living. Now, it’s the GOP that looks more focused on transgender people than the price of diesel and food. 

Iowa’s conservative lean might still save Hinson and some Republicans in the state. But if the top-ticket Republicans lose, they will have few people other than Trump to blame for losing a state that he had secured in their column for the past decade.
news.summary: Analysis: A Republican Senate candidate is struggling to separate herself from Trump’s ‘forever wars,’ Eric Garcia writes. Democrats see an opening in that quandary

A growing faction on the right is embracing something that looks increasingly like socialism, or, at minimum, has become far too comfortable wielding federal power in ways that should be off-limits to a movement committed to shrinking government and limiting its reach. 

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz called out that faction Tuesday, officially labeling its members RINOs, who offer voters little beyond the same government benefits and economic intervention long associated with the left, only redirected toward a different set of favored constituents. "Look, I agree with you. There are people that are selling this siren sign, and it's an interesting beast. We used to have a couple of decades ago what would be called RINOs," the Texas Senator said. "It's essentially weak Republicans, Republicans in name only, that would say, we're going to spend money too, we just won't give away as much as the Democrats. Today, instead of coming from the moderate, mushy middle, where that urge is coming from is the self-declared populist."

"Look, I'll be clear, I consider myself very much a populist. The base that has elected me every time has been blue-collar workers. Here's the difference. Cruz said. "Bernie Sanders and Kamala Harris's tax policy and economic policy does not work. And you are right, there are some misguided voices in MAGA saying, let's embrace socialism lite. Reviewing official records, MS NOW reported that a new Trump-affiliated PAC, Never Go Back, has already spent $6 million on GOP races in districts that the president carried by double digits in the 2024 election. The report called this the latest sign that the midterms "are shaping up to be a potential disaster for the GOP," alongside polling that consistently shows recently redrawn districts "don’t appear to be safe" from an impending blue wave.

"[The] biggest investment among the ruby red redrawn districts so far is in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, where Federal Election Commission filings show No Going Back PAC spending more than $2 million on a combination of TV ads and mailers," the report continued. "In that district, Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is facing off against Republican Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton. While Florida’s 25th district backed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by approximately 5 points, Florida Republicans redrew the map to turn the area into a Trump +9.2 district. And yet, despite the new district lines, Moskowitz looks like he could pull off the upset. On Tuesday, Fox News moved its rating of the race from 'Toss-up' to 'Lean D.'" 

“The American way of life has become unaffordable,” Moskowitz said in a recent statement. “The Trump administration knows this, so their PAC will spend hundreds of millions of dollars to run ads to change the topic. But the bill always comes due at the end of the month.”

news.title: El-Sayed asked the right question. America hasn't found the answer | Opinion
news.text:
“Birth should be joyful.”

That’s how VP Kamala Harris opened a conversation about Black maternal healthcare at Birth Detroit on Sept. 22. I had the honor to watch as Mini Timmaraju, president and CEO of Reproductive Freedom for All, moderated a table of Black women, Harris and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. They talked about the care Black women deserve, the care they actually receive and the work still ahead.

Here in Michigan, Black babies were nearly three times as likely as white babies to die before their first birthday in 2023. Those numbers should stop us in our tracks. Instead, we keep asking Black women to live with a level of risk we would never accept for everyone else.

El-Sayed asked a question in his opening remarks that has stayed with me: “What would we build if we treated all of our kids like all of our kids?”

Leseliey Welch, one of the women who co-founded Birth Detroit, talked about her goal of making midwifery care available in every community. She also talked about what her organization calls “beloved birth”: care centered on families, led by midwives working with physicians and rooted in the community. Care that treats patients and providers with dignity.

El-Sayed shared that he has worked alongside Welch for more than a decade. He talked about how amazing it is to grow up, and watch your friends grow up. I loved that. Here was Welch, building the care she wants families to have, sitting alongside Kamala Harris and El-Sayed, who has been rolling up his sleeves in his own work to help communities get better care, too. He knows her work because he has spent years doing this work alongside her.

More from Freep Opinion: Trump says 2026 is about him. Michigan voters should believe him.

The presence of so many advocates in the room made the moment feel bigger than one conversation. These women have been pushing for better Black maternal health care for decades. They are building what families need, while still having to confront the failures baked into the system.

But while they’re building better care, Black women are still dying from causes we know how to prevent. Danielle Atkinson of Mothering Justice talked about Amber Nicole Thurman and Candi Miller, two Black women who lost their lives. Two deaths that Georgia’s maternal mortality review committee deemed completely preventable.

That’s when I started crying.

What will prevent the next death?

Because how do we talk about these women and still look around at a country that continues to fail Black women and people giving birth? What is going to prevent the next woman from dying? What have we actually done to improve Black maternal health, specifically?

More from Freep Opinion: John James' running mate just put abortion back on the ballot

I’ve worked in ob/gyn care for more than a decade, and I’ve given birth to three children myself. I know how vulnerable it can feel to trust someone with your body and your baby. I also know, as a white woman, that I have not had to carry the same risks as the women at that table.

Paula Thornton Greear, President and CEO of Planned Parenthood of Michigan, said something I haven’t stopped thinking about: While we sit here talking, more Black women will die. And in this country, we’ve allowed that to become normal.

Shanay Watson-Whitaker of Reproductive Freedom for All talked about Planned Parenthood health centers closing across Michigan, from Marquette to Warren. And when a clinic closes, the people who need care don’t disappear.Michiganders voted to protect reproductive rights through Proposal 3 in 2022. But a right on paper doesn’t mean much if you can’t find a provider or get to a clinic. I’ve spent years teaching patients how to advocate for themselves, and I believe in that deeply. You can’t advocate for yourself if there’s nowhere to go for care.

Conversation isn't enough

That’s what I wish people understood about reproductive justice. Yes, I advocate for abortion access, and I get plenty of hateful messages for it. But I advocate for access to all reproductive healthcare. I want people to be able to build their families how they want, when they want and with whom they want. And I want them to have the care and support to make it through pregnancy, birth and everything that comes after.

Harris said conversations like this bring Black maternal health into the consciousness of people who don’t already think about it. That matters. But the women who sat at this table have been thinking about it for years. They have been caring for patients, building services, organizing and begging the rest of us to see what is happening.

El-Sayed said “we have to fight with love.” To me, that means listening to the Black women who have been doing this work for decades, using what I know as a clinician, and calling in other white people who may not yet see this as their fight, too. It means showing up for the hard conversations and staying for the work that follows.

The women at that table are building better care in so many different ways: in clinics, in communities, through advocacy and through policy. They’ve been doing the work. Now the rest of us need to show up alongside them, in every place where we have the power to change what happens next.

Nikki Sapiro Vinckier, PA-C, is a Michigan-based reproductive health advocate, OB-GYN Physician Associate and author of We Deserve More: Why Reproductive Healthcare Is Broken and What You Can Do About It. She is the founder of Take Back Trust, a nonprofit dedicated to helping people navigate reproductive healthcare with greater clarity and confidence. You can find her online @nikkivinck . news.title: Poll: Most voters agree the 2026 midterms are all about Trump — and they disapprove
news.text:
By a 12-point margin, registered voters say they'd prefer to elect a Democrat to Congress over a Republican, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll.

The poll finds more voters think Democrats would do a better job dealing with gas prices, the economy, and foreign policy than Republicans amid rising prices and the war in Iran. A majority also say it is more important to back candidates with new ideas who will bring about change than those with experience and a proven record.

President Trump continues to sit at near record low approval ratings, with just 39% approving of his job and the highest share of strong disapproval — 53% — since the question was first asked in 2017.

In the final weeks of the 2026 campaign, Democrats have a notable edge in voter enthusiasm and support from independents as a building wave of backlash to the party in power comes into focus.

The survey of 1,280 respondents was conducted September 14-15 and has a margin of error of +/- 3.8 percentage points, meaning results could be about 3.8 points higher or lower. Respondents were reached by live caller, text and online.

Trump on the ballot

"I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot," Trump told Republicans at an unprecedented midterm convention in Dallas earlier this month. Many voters seem to have taken Trump's insistence to heart.

A plurality of voters (45%) say their choice for Congress is a vote against President Trump, including four in five Democrats and about half of independents. About a quarter of voters — including 59% of Republicans and 51% of Trump 2024 voters — say their vote is about supporting the president.

About a third of voters say that Trump is not much of a factor in their choices, and 41% of those are Republican.

Overall, registered voters say they were more likely to pick a Democratic candidate for Congress than a Republican, 53% to 41%. This marks a 13-point swing from how much Trump won the 2024 popular vote by and is one of the reasons that House districts and Senate races in solidly conservative areas are competitive this fall.

The double-digit swing highlights the potential disparity in voter enthusiasm that could see Democrats regain control of the House and even the Senate. Trump 2024 voters are more likely to say they are not following the midterm election closely than those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris. They are also less likely to care as much about who wins control of Congress and less likely to have been contacted by someone encouraging them to vote in the election.

These dynamics are one reason why Democrats are competitive in Senate races held in states where Trump won big in 2024 like Ohio (11 points), Alaska (13 points), Iowa (13 points) and Texas (14 points) that could give them a majority in that chamber.

Republicans lose advantage on key issues

More than a year and a half into Trump's return to office, a solid majority of voters (59%) continue to disapprove of the president's performance in office while 39% approve.

Overall disapproval has remained the same since May but the intensity of that disapproval has increased: 53% of voters strongly disapprove, the highest mark recorded at any point during Trump's two terms. Since his return to office, Trump has been viewed less favorably by voters, too, from a 44% favorability rating in January 2025 to just 37% today.

The Republican Party has lost its advantage on several key issues in the eyes of voters, including immigration: 41% say the Democratic Party would do better while 38% say Republicans. In February 2024, it was 42% for Republicans and 30% for Democrats.

By a wider margin, voters also think Democrats would be better for the economy (42% to 38%), gas prices (40% to 27%) and foreign policy (42% to 36%). These four are top issues for the midterms and where Republican candidates have begun to break with Trump.

Last week Florida Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents a district where Trump won by more than 14 points in 2024, released a campaign ad telling the president "some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far."

This week, Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson and former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers, both Republican Senate nominees, reversed their positions to come out in favor of ending the Iran war and called for suspension of gas taxes to combat rising prices.

According to AAA data, the statewide average for diesel fuel is more than $6.31 a gallon in Iowa and $6.88 in Michigan, both the highest record average prices in their tracking history.
news.summary: A new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds President Trump — and his unpopularity — is an outsize factor in why most voters say they want Democrats to win the midterms.

news.title: Republicans redrew their districts to make them safe. Now they’re spending millions to defend them.
news.text:
When Republicans redrew congressional districts in a number of states over the last year, they hoped their efforts would maximize GOP House seats and minimize the number of contests where Democrats could feasibly win.

But now, with just weeks to go before Election Day, Republicans are suddenly finding a host of deep red districts in play — and President Donald Trump’s political operation is now spending millions to defend Republicans in a dozen districts that the GOP redrew to favor Trump by at least nine percentage points. 

In fact, if these maps existed in 2024, Trump would have carried these districts by an average of 12 points.

Records reviewed by MS NOW show that so far, No Going Back PAC — a new super PAC tied to Trump’s political operation — has already invested approximately $6 million in redrawn districts where the Republican has a roughly double-digit advantage based on Trump’s 2024 performance.

It’s the latest sign of a larger problem for Republicans: The midterms are shaping up to be a potential disaster for the GOP.

Polling suggests the maps that were designed to protect the Republican majority from a blue wave don’t appear to be safe, and Republicans are now compelled to spend in districts that should be solidly red.

No Going Back PAC and MAGA, Inc. — the primary Trump-affiliated campaign organization — did not immediately respond to MS NOW’s request for comment on their spending decisions.But the biggest investment among the ruby red redrawn districts so far is in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, where Federal Election Commission filings show No Going Back PAC spending more than $2 million on a combination of TV ads and mailers.

In that district, Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz is facing off against Republican Scott Singer, the former mayor of Boca Raton. While Florida’s 25th district backed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by approximately 5 points, Florida Republicans redrew the map to turn the area into a Trump +9.2 district.

And yet, despite the new district lines, Moskowitz looks like he could pull off the upset. On Tuesday, Fox News moved its rating of the race from “Toss-up” to “Lean D.”In a statement, Moskowitz mocked No Going Back PAC’s investment. “The American way of life has become unaffordable,” Moskowitz said. “The Trump administration knows this, so their PAC will spend hundreds of millions of dollars to run ads to change the topic.”

“But,” Moskowitz added, “the bill always comes due at the end of the month.”

Singer’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Of course, Texas Republicans first kicked off the mid-decade redistricting war — at Trump’s urging — last summer. Other states followed suit, including North Carolina, Ohio and Florida, with state lawmakers crafting new maps aimed at advantaging the GOP.

Democrats responded in kind, with redistricting initiatives in California and Virginia.

On the GOP side of the battle, however, Republicans are still having to spend in these districts to support the GOP candidates. For example, federal filings show that Trump-affiliated groups have poured in more than $1 million in Texas’s 35th Congressional District, which backed Harris by more than 30 points in 2024. (The district now favors Trump by about 10 points, after Republicans spread out the GOP advantage elsewhere.)

But it’s not just districts in Texas that became more Democratic.

No Going Back PAC is investing more than $500,000 on a TV ad in Texas’ 34th Congressional District, which was redrawn into a Trump +10 district.

And the group is spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on campaign mailers and other voter outreach efforts across districts like Alabama’s 2nd (Trump +14.3), Florida’s 22nd (Trump +10.6), North Carolina’s 1st (Trump +11.6) and Ohio’s 15th (Trump +10).

In a statement, the spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee accused Republicans of “running scared.” 

“By lighting their money on fire almost entirely in defensive districts and in places Trump won by double digits two years ago, MAGA Inc. is signaling that vulnerable House Republicans are in deep trouble and poised to lose,” DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said.

A spokesperson for House Majority PAC —which also works to elect Democrats to the House — argued in a statement that “strong” candidates are expanding the “battlefield deep into Trump territory.”

“Now Trump and Republicans are being forced to spend millions defending deep-red districts, including seats they literally redrew to make safer for themselves earlier this cycle,” spokesperson Katarina Flicker said. “This spending is the clearest evidence yet that Democratic recruitment has fundamentally changed the House map.”

Although the spending is just the latest sign that Republicans could be in trouble come November, GOP operatives downplayed the significance of the support.

While true that every dollar spent in what should be a safe Republican district can’t go to help a more vulnerable Republican, the GOP has a sizable money advantage this fall that makes these spending decisions less consequential. There is, mathematically, just more money to go around for Republicans.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the House GOP’s campaign arm — the National Republican Congressional Committee, which legally cannot be involved in the Trump-affiliated PAC’s spending decisions — sought to put GOP-aligned campaign spending in broader context, casting Democrats as broadly outspent in competitive districts across the board.

Data shared shows Republicans overall outspending Democrats on TV and digital ad buys in the more competitive districts, where Harris or Trump won in 2024 by less than 10 points. Democrats have — so far — been spending more than the Republicans in the districts carried by either candidate by more than 10 points.

“Republicans have air superiority,” NRCC Spokesman Mike Marinella said in a statement.

“House Democrats are scrambling to catch up with the very limited resources they have,” he said.

news.title: AI anxiety is sweeping the globe — and cutting across party lines: poll
news.text: The freakout over AI that started in Silicon Valley and led to growing American calls to pause development has swept Western countries. A new POLITICO Poll finds that pluralities of adults in the US, Canada, and Europe want to pause AI development regardless of their political leanings — and most believe there's a real risk the technology could destroy humanity. Pluralities of respondents in several countries say it's okay for their country to fall behind others in the development of AI if it means being more responsible and secure when advancing it. And they're more likely to expect AI will destroy jobs rather than create them. The results from the poll, conducted by independent polling firm Public First, illustrate the sheer magnitude of how AI fears are spreading as some industry leaders warn the technology's advancement could have potentially grave consequences. They show people's preference for caution, even at the risk of forfeiting what could be revolutionary advancements or their country falling behind in the broader AI race. And for governments, the results offer a stark warning of the political backlash they may face if they don't take steps to rein in the technology, as leaders from US President Donald Trump to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham scramble their responses. Across six countries — the US, Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Spain, and Germany — roughly half of adults surveyed said AI is good enough now, so they supported a pause on further development to reduce risks, rather than continuing development for added benefits. That sentiment was highest in the UK at 51% and lowest in Germany at 45%. Meanwhile, just 30% to 40% of adults in each country favored continued development to bring about "significant benefits." An even greater share of adults — more than half in every country surveyed and up to almost two-thirds in the US, France, the UK, and Canada — said there was at least a "moderate" risk that the technology could "destroy humanity." The skepticism around AI could impact Europe's ability to keep up in the global competition: The European Union, which has taken a cautionary approach by adopting the world's first AI regulation in 2024, hosts almost no providers of frontier AI models, with French Mistral as the most worthy contender. The bloc's highest official, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, leaned into the calls for a pause, saying during her yearly address last week that "if the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too." She's invited the main AI labs to talk about how the EU could "support" industry efforts to pace the frontier. But the recent AI warnings have put European policymakers in a tough spot, as the EU spent most of last year focusing on catching up in the race by preparing to invest billions in compute capacity and trying to boost low AI adoption rates. European policymakers faced additional pressure from activists on Monday, when the Pause AI movement demonstrated in front of the European Parliament buildings in Brussels. "We would not board a plane with a one-in-ten-chance of exploding mid-air," said Didier Coeurnelle, the coordinator of PauseAI Belgium, referring to the recent assessment from an Anthropic employee that there's a higher than 10% chance AI could wipe out humanity. "That is what we are tolerating with AI today." Calls for slowing AI development have gone mainstream after AI titans including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk raised the idea in recent days. Consensus on the issue quickly fell apart in America after Trump blasted the AI warnings as a "HOAX," sinking the likelihood of an immediate bipartisan deal to regulate AI. Since then, other industry leaders including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and former White House adviser David Sacks have similarly downplayed the technology's dangers and resisted calls for new government regulations, blaming alarmists for overinflating AI risks. "This poll fits the classic techno-panic pattern: few harms today, plenty of fear about tomorrow," said Neil Chilson, head of AI policy at the U.S.-based Abundance Institute. Chilson pointed to the POLITICO Poll finding that in every country but Spain, a third of respondents — or more — had rarely or never used AI. "Most people haven't felt AI's benefits but they've heard many scary stories about its future," he added. "For now, fear is outrunning experience. But experience will catch up." Still, many Republican and Democratic state leaders have scrambled to push for stronger controls, defying Trump's and the federal government's hands-off approach. In California, the global epicenter of the AI industry, politicians are also tightening regulations as voters there sour on the technology. On Friday, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom — a likely 2028 presidential candidate — signed an executive order accelerating the implementation of new AI oversight standards and tasked state agencies with exploring whether a mandatory "kill switch" is needed for the most advanced AI models. As politicians in America and beyond heed the warnings, so too, do voters. According to the poll, people across North America and Europe view industry researchers' warnings as legitimate. When asked whether AI lab staff really believed their own fears that "AI will kill us all" or if they were making a "marketing move" to hype their products, adults from all six countries tended to view the warnings as genuine. That's despite a suggestion among some industry observers that frontier AI companies may have sought to benefit from the publicity around their models. "I think a lot of it is marketing, to overemphasize the proposed capabilities," Max Junestrand, co-founder and CEO of Legora, an American-Swedish AI firm valued at over $5 billion, said in an interview when asked about this summer's AI hacking incidents. Wariness of rapid AI development and its risks to society mostly crossed party lines in Europe and Canada. In the US, it was slightly more partisan: Americans who had voted for Trump in 2024 split almost evenly when asked whether to pause advanced AI development (44%) or press forward (40%), and they were more inclined than those who voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 to say that AI employees' alarmist talk was a marketing stunt. Nearly half of Trump voters also said the US shouldn't allow itself to fall behind other countries in the AI development race, even if it means taking risks to stay ahead. In comparison, majorities in Canada and the UK (53%) opted for falling behind on AI advancement to prioritize security, even if it meant potentially ceding a technological edge to other countries. Tyler Katzenberger reported from Sacramento, California, and Pieter Haeck reported from Brussels. This edition of The POLITICO Poll was conducted by Public First from Sept. 13 to 15, surveying more than 2,000 respondents each from the U.S., Canada, U.K., France, Spain and Germany, and has an overall margin of error of ±2.2 percentage points. Smaller subgroups have higher margins of error. This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms.

news.text:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has seen his personal fortune grow by more than $1 billion since he took office in 2019, according to a new estimate.

The Hyatt hotel heir has also fueled speculation about a possible presidential campaign after opening up about the significant health changes he has been pursuing.

Forbes estimates that Pritzker is now worth approximately $4.2 billion, placing him among the names featured on the magazine’s 2026 World’s Billionaires list.

His wealth climbed by more than $500 million over the past year alone. Despite that increase, Pritzker fell from 979th to 1,108th among the world’s wealthiest people.

If elected president, he would become the second billionaire in a row to hold the office, following Donald Trump.

Much of Pritzker’s fortune comes from his family’s hotel empire. He also previously led a private equity firm with his brother before leaving the business in 2017.

The Pritzker family ranks among America’s most powerful wealthy dynasties, with 13 family members currently recognized as billionaires.

Our News Outlet has contacted Gov. Pritzker for comment.

Pritzker has disclosed that he began taking a GLP-1 medication two years ago after receiving a diabetes diagnosis.

The 61-year-old Democrat said the treatment has helped him lose 80 pounds. In a Monday interview with CBS, he said he feels “a whole lot different and a whole lot better.”

He said his concerns about the health risks of being overweight were shaped in part by the death of his father, who suffered a fatal heart attack at age 39.

“He was actually quite an active person, even though he was overweight, and so he was on a tennis court and had a heart attack, and my mother was there, and he died in her arms,” Pritzker said.

Pritzker said the demands of public office contributed to further weight gain. His size has also made him a frequent target of mockery from Trump.

“Pritzker, I don’t know, he’s too busy eating,” Trump said at a 2024 campaign rally. “He wants to eat all the time.”

His doctor prescribed the medication after blood tests conducted two years ago showed that Pritzker had diabetes.

“My doctor said, ‘Oh, no, you’ll never come off of it. You’re going to have to do this the rest of your life, and I recommend that you take a GLP-1,’” Pritzker recalled.

He said the effects were noticeable almost immediately, with a two-pound loss during his first week and a marked reduction in his appetite.

“All of a sudden, on the third day, I was like, you know, actually, I don’t need to eat that thing,” Pritzker said.

‘But it was the strangest feeling. Now, I’m not suggesting everything changed in a week. It didn’t happen that way.’

GLP-1s mimic a naturally occurring gut hormone, helping regulate blood sugar and curb appetite by slowing digestion and increasing feelings of fullness. They are used to treat type 2 diabetes and, in some formulations, obesity.

Common brand names include Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide, as well as Mounjaro and Zepbound, which contain tirzepatide, a related dual GIP/GLP-1 drug. 

The governor announced that Illinois is covering GLP-1s on the state insurance plan for 55,000 civil servants and says that the drug will save money by preventing other diseases.

As well as the drug, Pritzker says that he takes a four-mile walk each morning along Lake Michigan to help keep the weight off.

Asked if he was working on his image ahead of a 2028 presidential run, Pritzker replied: ‘I’ve been driven my whole life to lose weight. The fact that I am now able to do it because this GLP-1 became available is truly, like, I mean, it’s something that has meant a lot to me.

‘I have not made any decisions about what I might do in the future. I can tell you I want to be the governor of the state of Illinois for a while longer, and I’m running for reelection.’

The latest Democratic 2028 polling puts Pritzker well behind the early front-runners, despite persistent speculation that the billionaire Illinois governor could mount a White House bid.

A September Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll had Kamala Harris on 17 percent, narrowly ahead of Pete Buttigieg on 16 percent, with Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez both on 14 percent. Pritzker was not among the candidates registering support in the poll’s leading tier.

A separate Harvard CAPS/Harris survey earlier this month placed Pritzker at 4 percent, behind Harris on 42 percent, Newsom on 18 percent, Buttigieg and Ocasio-Cortez on 9 percent apiece, and Josh Shapiro and Jon Ossoff on 7 percent.

news.title: CNN’s polling guru calls the 2028 Democratic field a ‘mess’
news.text:
Democratic voters remain deeply divided over a potential nominee for the 2028 presidential race, according to new polling from Bowling Green State University and YouGov.

The survey placed former Vice President Kamala Harris in a tight race at the top of a crowded pack, with 17 percent support among Democratic voters.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg closely followed at 16 percent, while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and California Governor Gavin Newsom polled at 14 percent each.

Reviewing the data on “CNN News Central,” CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten described the early primary landscape as exceptionally scattered, comparing the party’s primary base to people who “don’t know what the heck they want.”

“There are four folks within 17 percent, I mean, it’s just completely messy,” Enten said. “The clear thing to take away here is there is no clear leader in this group. This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years. I would argue, the messiest, least clear Democratic field since 1992.”

Enten noted that the current primary environment differs significantly from prior cycles, calling the lineup the party’s “messiest” in decades and joking that “it’s messier than an airport the Sunday after Thanksgiving.”

Addressing Harris’s standing, CNN host Kate Bolduan asked how her current support compared with her earlier popularity among Democrats. Enten highlighted her sharp drop in numbers since the summer of 2024.

“You see the 17 percent now, back in July of 2024, just as Joe Biden was getting out of the race, Kamala Harris was polling at 45 percent,” Enten said. “You know, that’s more than twice as much as the support that she has right now.”

Enten compared her position with President Donald Trump’s early lead ahead of the 2024 Republican primary, when Trump held 49 percent support among GOP voters.

“This is a weak place for a frontrunner,” Enten said. “These are the types of numbers that would really make me think twice about running if I was Kamala Harris, given her universal name recognition.”

The polling metrics were released hours before Harris was scheduled to join Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a campaign stop in Michigan. 

The trip to the battleground state reignited questions about her potential 2028 plans, though Harris has not publicly announced or committed to another campaign.
news.summary: Four potential candidates remain within three percentage points of each other at the top of new 2028 polling, led narrowly by former Vice President Kamala Harris

news.title: Kamala Harris Calls Trump’s Media Ban ‘Absolutely Abhorrent’
news.text:
Kamala Harris called President Donald Trump’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “absolutely abhorrent.”

On Tuesday, the former vice president was stopped while getting in a car by CBS News, among other outlets, and was asked what her thoughts were on the media ban. She replied while getting into her car.

“The man is afraid of the voice of the people and that the people understand and know what he’s doing,” Harris told CBS News’ Aaron Navarro. “He’s trying to stifle the ability of journalists to let the people of America know what’s really going on with their government.”

Watch her response below.

Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House grounds Friday. Reporters from the outlets were denied access to the White House on Saturday and CNN was removed from its duties as the White House pool representative for television networks on Monday. 

This backfired on the president Monday when CNN was slated to represent as the pool videographers for one of his events, but it could not be heard because the camera operators and sound people were not allowed on site. 

The five major television networks — Fox News Media, ABC News, CBS News, CNN and NBC News — that make up the White House TV pool suspended pooled television coverage of President Trump on Monday after the White House prevented CNN from fulfilling its scheduled duties.

The banned outlets noted that their access was removed “without notice or process” and that the move from the president threatens press freedom and “the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.” 

CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit against the president, arguing that he imposed the ban over what he sees as negative-only news media coverage. The case was assigned to a federal judge, who was nominated by Trump and previously sided with CNN when the White House attempted to expel one of its White House reporters in 2018. The organizations are seeking a temporary restraining order restoring their access.

The White House Correspondents’ Association also called on the Trump administration to restore the outlets’ access, saying the government should not determine which journalists can cover the president based on whether officials approve of their reporting.

news.title: Kamala Harris backs El-Sayed, says Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat is key
news.text:
Stressing the national importance of Michigan's role in the 2026 midterms, former Vice President and 2024 Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris stopped in Detroit and threw her support behind Abdul El-Sayed, Democrats' pick for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat.

She endorsed him at Birth Detroit, a community birth center in the city, at the conclusion of a roundtable with the nominee and reproductive health advocates. She said El-Sayed's race against Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake Township will impact affordable health care, childcare and housing.

"That's why I'm here, because these are the big issues that I know impact people across our country, including here in Michigan," she told reporters.

During the event, she recalled serving alongside now-retiring Michigan U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, D-Bloomfield Township, saying it gave her a sense of the weight of representing the battleground state.

"His will be a voice — Abdul's — that is a voice representing the people of this state, and it will be a national voice," she said, according to a Fox 2 livestream of the discussion.

During the discussion with Harris on Black maternal health disparities, El-Sayed, who previously served as the health director for Detroit and Wayne County, said his race is about one question — inspired by the venue: "What would we build if we treated all of our kids like all of our kids?" he said.

Ahead of the roundtable, Rogers had characterized Harris' visit as a sign that his Democratic rival's campaign is flailing.

"Desperate times call for desperate measures, and Abdul is so desperate that he’s parachuting Kamala Harris into Michigan to save his flailing campaign," Rogers said in statement.

El-Sayed brushed off the attack when a reporter asked him about it before his meeting with Harris and the others.

"You know what a desperate measure is? Pretending like you didn't back a war that you've been backing for seven months now, calling it a 'win-win-win' then looking at your poll numbers and being like, 'Maybe that was a bad idea,'" he said, referring to Rogers' recent call for the war in Iran to "end quickly."

More: Rabbis ask Kamala Harris to talk to Abdul El-Sayed about their concerns

More: Michigan AG Dana Nessel says she will vote for El-Sayed for Senate

Besides highlighting the national importance of Michigan's open Senate race, Harris' appearance could help El-Sayed boost support among Black voters — a traditionally reliable Democratic voting bloc — who backed his primary opponent in the primary.

In Detroit, Michigan's largest majority-Black city, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham secured 62% of the vote to El-Sayed's 34% in August.

Rogers' campaign had a truck outside the roundtable event trying to paint El-Sayed as racist, even as he campaigned inside with the first woman of color to become a major political party's presidential nominee, and a group discussing Black women's health issues.

El-Sayed's primary served as a kind of litmus test for the brand of progressive politics he espouses, including his calls for Medicare for All and ending unconditional military aid to Israel.

Now, all eyes are on his race against Rogers, who has the endorsement of President Donald Trump, to see if El-Sayed’s platform carries broad appeal.

"Kamala Harris was a failed vice president who oversaw a massive influx of tens of millions of people into America illegally and ran on vibes rather than making Americans’ lives better," Onwuka added. "It was not their looks or gender but their policies and personalities that America rejected." "I think Joy Behar is taking a very complicated election and giving it a very simple explanation," psychotherapist and author Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital. "Two women lost to Donald Trump. That doesn’t prove Americans won’t elect a woman. It proves those two women lost those two elections. Sexism may have played a role for some voters, but you can’t take millions of votes and diagnose all of them as sexism." KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY During an episode of "The View" in July, Behar told her co-hosts, "Think of a woman that could win. Tell me one woman." During another episode of the show that month, Behar rejected Harris as a potential 2028 candidate. "I love her, she was great, but she didn't win one time. What makes you think she's going to win again?" Behar asked, adding that anyone who thought Harris should run again and could win was not living in reality. During an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., said she was weighing a presidential run in 2028, adding, "Pretty candidly, I think about my identity." "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina," she said. "And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities."
