news.title: AOC Says She Will Consider 2028 Presidential Run After Midterms: 'Every Element' Is Under Consideration'
news.text: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez appears to be weighing a potential 2028 presidential campaign, saying she expects to confront the decision after the midterm elections.In an unusually candid interview with The New York Times, the New York Democrat described the approaching decision as potentially a once-in-a-career opportunity. "There's an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot," Ocasio-Cortez said. "Life doesn't wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you."Ocasio-Cortez, 36, has represented New York's 14th Congressional District, which includes parts of the Bronx and Queens, since 2019, after stunning the Democratic establishment by defeating longtime Rep. Joe Crowley in the 2018 primary. Her choices for 2028 could include remaining in the House, seeking the New York Senate seat currently held by Chuck Schumer, or launching a campaign for president."Every element of this is something that's within consideration," she told the outlet. The congresswoman also addressed questions surrounding whether a Latina woman could win the presidency, pointing to the country's history of never electing a woman as president."I think about my identity," she said. "I'm not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina," Ocasio-Cortez said she considers those factors when thinking about a White House campaign but does not view them as making such a run impossible."This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she said, in reference to the defeats of Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Kamala Harris in 2024. Ocasio-Cortez said she has discussed gender in politics with Harris, though she declined to reveal details of their private conversations.A presidential bid would carry another significant consequence. House members face elections every two years, meaning Ocasio-Cortez could not return to her congressional seat if she abandoned it to run for president and lost."It's very all or nothing," she said. "If I were to run in this cycle, and not win, I would be done." She added that she was "not opposed" to that possibility but said a campaign would have to make the risk worthwhile.Ocasio-Cortez also left open the possibility of challenging Schumer, 75, who has not announced his plans for 2028. Asked whether she would defer to Schumer or other prominent Democrats when making her decision, she rejected that idea. "I don't think that my decisions would come down to deference," she said.Any national campaign would begin with Ocasio-Cortez possessing a substantial fundraising network. Federal Election Commission records show her congressional campaign reported more than $32.6 million in receipts between January 2025 and June 30, 2026, including nearly $32 million in individual contributions. The campaign ended that period with almost $16 million in cash on hand.Her deliberations also come as Democrats debate the party's ideological direction. Ocasio-Cortez remains one of Congress' most prominent progressive lawmakers and has been closely aligned with Sen. Bernie Sanders, whose presidential campaigns built a national coalition on the Democratic left.The two joined forces for the "Fighting Oligarchy" tour in 2025, an experience Ocasio-Cortez said demonstrated how their political constituencies could overlap while also bringing different voters into the same coalition."These rallies were bigger than the sum of their parts," she told the Times.Yet Ocasio-Cortez framed her eventual decision less around acquiring a particular office than around where she believes she can advance her policy agenda most effectively. She recalled remarks she made earlier this year that her ambition was not centered on "a title or a seat," but on issues including healthcare, wages and workers' rights. That question, she indicated, will ultimately shape whatever comes next after the 2026 midterms. "Where can I do the most good?" Ocasio-Cortez said.
news.author: Matias Civita

news.title: US ex-VP Harris campaigns for leftist El-Sayed in key Senate race
news.text:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (left) and former US vice president Kamala Harris take part in a reproductive health roundtable discussion in Detroit. (AFP pic)
MICHIGAN: Former US vice president Kamala Harris returned to the campaign trail Tuesday alongside a leftist Michigan Senate candidate, seeking to help Democrats hold a crucial battleground seat as speculation persists over another White House run in 2028.
Harris appeared with Abdul El-Sayed at a Detroit-area roundtable on Black maternal health and was scheduled to join other events aimed at mobilising voters in a state central to Democratic hopes of winning control of the Senate in November.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, faces Republican former congressman Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by a retiring Democrat.
A Republican victory would make an already challenging Democratic path to a Senate majority considerably steeper.
"The Senate should be a stopgap on the abuses of this administration, and I would suggest to you that the fellow sitting to my right would be one of them when elected," Harris said at the roundtable as she introduced the candidate to the cameras.
The epidemiologist has run in part on his experience in health administration, and he described maternal care as "personal" for him, revealing that two of his father's siblings died before turning five.
"Babies shouldn't die, full stop. And a measure of a society is... the choices we make about the services we provide, about the resources we offer, about the voices we listen to, about the perspective we share or don't share," said El-Sayed.
"Those are the markers of a society, and we have an opportunity in this race to decide that we are going to invest in health care."
The visit put Harris back in the spotlight in Michigan, where Donald Trump narrowly defeated her in the 2024 presidential election and which is set to vote early in the Democratic presidential nominating calendar in 2028.
Harris has said she is "thinking about" another presidential bid but has given no timeline for a decision.
Her Michigan appearance kicks off a broader burst of midterm campaigning, with stops also planned in Nevada and Georgia.
Tuesday's joint appearance was significant for El-Sayed as he seeks to unite Democrats after defeating establishment-backed Representative Haley Stevens in a bruising primary.
El-Sayed drew strong support from the left but performed less strongly among Black voters, a key Democratic constituency in Detroit that Harris's visit could help him reach.
The two Democrats have also occupied different ground over Israel.
El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel and US arms sales to the country, initially backed the "Uncommitted" protest movement against then-president Joe Biden during the 2024 Democratic primary.
Harris, as Biden's vice president, faced anger from Arab and Muslim voters in Michigan over the administration's support for Israel during the Gaza war.
She was also due Tuesday to meet Detroit faith leaders and attend a voter-turnout event involving the local branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People.
news.summary: Kamala Harris returns to the campaign trail to help Democrats hold a crucial Michigan seat as speculation persists over a 2028 White House run.
news.author: AFP

news.title: The Democrats Have a 2028 Problem
news.text:
Republicans have the luxury of a deep bench. Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and a roster of successful GOP governors give the party real options and a clear direction. Democrats have a crowded stage, and nobody is standing in the spotlight.

The closest thing the Democrats have for a frontrunner is Kamala Harris, and her frontrunner status is superficial at best.

On Tuesday, CNN chief data analyst Harry Enten walked through new 2028 polling, and when anchor Kate Bolduan asked him where Kamala Harris stands, Enten started with the voters themselves.

"[The Democratic base] don't know what the heck they want," Enten said. "This field is historically messy. It's messier than an airport Sunday after Thanksgiving."

The data backs him up. Kamala may lead the pack, but she leads it with a meager 17%. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg sits right behind her at 16%, while Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) each pull 14%. That puts four candidates within three points of one another.

"The clear thing to take away here is there is no clear leader in this group," Enten added. "This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years, I would argue, the messiest, least clear Democratic field since 1992."

ICYMI: The Somali Daycare Fraud Story Just Got Way Bigger Than Minnesota

The bigger story is Kamala's weak performance. In July 2024, just as Joe Biden bowed out of the race, she polled at 45% as Democrats' top choice for the nomination. Today she's at 17%, which means she has shed well over half of her support. Think about that for a second. This is the woman with universal name recognition, the former vice president and a woman of color no less, and the best head start of anyone in the party, and her numbers keep going down. She may be ahead, but her lead is not secure.

Enten offered a useful comparison. "What you really want to be is more where Trump was at this point. Back in the 2024 cycle, he was at 49%," he said. "49% is not anything like 17%. This is a weak place for a frontrunner."

Then he delivered the kicker. "These are the types of numbers that would really make me think twice about running," Enten said.

I still say she is going to run. And her best option is to declare early. But she’s clearly doing some 2028 positioning. The poll dropped just hours before Kamala headed to Michigan to appear alongside Socialist Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for some roundtable event. Appearing with El-Sayed, especially when many establishment Democrats are keeping their distance, is a clear 2028 flex, even though she hasn't announced a campaign or publicly committed to running again.

No clear leader in Democrat 2028 field."This is a field that is messier than any Democratic field in at least 20 years. I would argue, the messiest, least clear democratic field since 1992.” —Harry Enten pic.twitter.com/9YNMrjVfrp— Matt Margolis (@mattmargolis) September 22, 2026

This is a structural problem for the left, and a bad news cycle won't explain it away. The party's pseudo frontrunner is basically neck and neck with several other candidates. Republicans will head into 2028 choosing between strong options. Democrats have had a long time to figure out who they want to lead their party into the future and they still don’t know. So, they will head into 2028 still trying to figure out what they want, and right now, even their own voters can't tell them.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: Kamala Harris Campaigns With El-Sayed in High-Stakes Michigan Senate Race
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris stumped in Detroit on Sept. 22 for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, hoping to boost the fellow Democrat’s chances of winning in November and the party’s odds of retaking the U.S. Senate.

The two appeared together Tuesday afternoon at a roundtable hosted by Birth Detroit, a black-led community birth center and maternal health provider that has endorsed El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race against former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.

Harris told the panel that she was there to support El-Sayed, a former Wayne County Health director, because she knows he will “be a champion” for maternal healthcare, particularly for black Americans.

The former vice president highlighted how the United States has one of the highest maternal mortality rates in the developed world, and that black women are more than three times more likely to die in childbirth compared to white women.

“Here are the facts that highlight the stakes in this election and the need to have a United States senator from the state of Michigan walking those halls, understanding the issue, and having the character and personality to be a fighter for the people who deserve to be seen, recognized, and treated with dignity,” Harris told the panel.

She criticized the One Big Beautiful Bill Act—signed by President Donald Trump in July 2025—for funding tax breaks with cuts to Medicaid, the largest payer of maternal and prenatal healthcare in the United States. Harris also hit Rogers for supporting that legislation.

The Rogers campaign did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

El-Sayed told the panel, “We need to make Medicaid whole again.”

“Yes, we need to replace the [Affordable Care Act] subsidies, but we need everybody to have the healthcare that they need and deserve,” El-Sayed said, referring to mothers.

El-Sayed has been making his pitch to Michigan voters with less than 50 days to go before the November election, appearing at rallies throughout the state, including a voter town hall in Saginaw on Saturday.

Harris endorsed El-Sayed almost immediately after he won the August primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), writing in a statement that “El-Sayed understands that the power is with the people, and that the stakes couldn’t be higher in this election.”

The progressive populist Democrat was also one of eight members of then-candidate Joe Biden’s 2020 Unity Task Force for Healthcare, a joint effort with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) after the latter lost to Biden in that year’s presidential primary.

El-Sayed was also an early supporter of the “uncommitted” movement that withheld support for Biden during the 2024 presidential primary over the former president’s record on Israel and Gaza.

However, he publicly endorsed Harris one day after Biden dropped out of the race and had made it clear months prior that his support for the “uncommitted” movement was strictly tied to the primary and was meant to send a message to the then-president, as Biden was overwhelmingly favored to clinch the nomination.

Democrats need to flip four seats to retake control of the U.S. Senate, but that number increases if they fail to hold onto any of the three races they’re defending on home turf: Michigan, New Hampshire, and Georgia.

In the latter, Democrats are hopeful that incumbent Sen. John Ossoff (D-Ga.), who continues to maintain a near 8-point lead in the RealClearPolitics polling average, will ultimately beat Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) in November and keep the Georgia seat in hand.

But Michigan is different. Trump narrowly won the state in 2016, and a progressive populist Democrat has never won statewide in what is one of the most purple battlegrounds nationwide. El-Sayed also barely beat Stevens in this year’s primary, winning by less than one percentage point after polls had put him up by double digits.

Even so, El-Sayed is facing Rogers, the Republican who lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) in the very same year (2024) when Trump managed to win statewide, and when Republicans enjoyed a favorable ballot advantage across the country.

Republicans also haven’t won a Michigan Senate race in more than 30 years, since then-Sen. Spencer Abraham (R-Mich.), won in 1994. Abraham lost his reelection bid to then-candidate Debbie Stabenow (D-Mich.) in 2000.

Currently, El-Sayed is leading Rogers by 2.8 percentage points in the RealClearPolitics polling average, while most surveys have given the progressive populist a slight advantage within the margin of error.
news.summary: The former vice president endorsed the progressive populist shortly after he won the August primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.).
news.author: Jacob Burg

news.title: Dem Star Drops Bombshell on 2028 Ambitions
news.text:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is openly weighing a 2028 run for either the White House or Senate.

The progressive congresswoman, 36, told The New York Times that she is doing mental “math” as she considers whether to launch a bid for either office.

Ocasio-Cortez has repeatedly been floated as a potential challenger to longtime New York Senator Chuck Schumer, whose seat is up for reelection in 2028, and has been the center of speculation regarding a possible presidential run. 

However, polls show that Ocasio-Cortez faces low favorability ratings that could hinder a future White House bid. In a July CNN/SSRS survey, the New York congresswoman’s national favorability rating stood at just around 26 percent, with her unfavorable rating as high as 36 percent.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she told The Times. “And you don’t—and just in life in general—life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

As she weighs her options, Ocasio-Cortez said she is also considering her identity and how it may impact her chances. 

“I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina,” she said. “And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities.”

Ocasio-Cortez made headlines over the summer with a series of candid Instagram posts announcing her decision to freeze her eggs. The decision drew backlash from Republicans, including MAGA influencer Laura Loomer, who called the move a “political stunt.” 

Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris’ losses were also front of mind for Ocasio-Cortez.

“This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” she said. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.”

Ocasio-Cortez told The Times that she had discussed a potential presidential campaign with Harris, who is also weighing a 2028 run, but declined to describe their conversations. 

The congresswoman also didn’t rule out challenging longtime New York senator Chuck Schumer, who has not announced whether he will run for reelection in 2028. 

Asked about whether she would still challenge Schumer if Democrats win back the Senate majority, Ocasio-Cortez said the decision wouldn’t “come down to deference.”
